heading: Preface
section_path: Distributed Systems: A Short Technical Primer > Preface
chunk_text: Distributed Systems: A Short Technical Primer > Preface\\n\\nPreface\\n\\nThis short primer introduces a small set of concepts used when describing distributed software. It is intentionally concise so that every expected structural element, entity mention, and relationship can be reviewed.

heading: 1.1 Distributed Systems
section_path: Distributed Systems: A Short Technical Primer > Chapter 1: Nodes and Communication > 1.1 Distributed Systems
chunk_text: Distributed Systems: A Short Technical Primer > Chapter 1: Nodes and Communication > 1.1 Distributed Systems\\n\\n1.1 Distributed Systems\\n\\nA **distributed system** is a collection of independent computing nodes that communicate to coordinate work. The nodes do not share one physical memory space.

heading: 1.2 Definition: Node
section_path: Distributed Systems: A Short Technical Primer > Chapter 1: Nodes and Communication > 1.2 Definition: Node
chunk_text: Distributed Systems: A Short Technical Primer > Chapter 1: Nodes and Communication > 1.2 Definition: Node\\n\\n1.2 Definition: Node\\n\\nA **node** is an independent computing participant in a distributed system. A node may be a physical machine or a software process.

heading: 1.3 Definition: Message
section_path: Distributed Systems: A Short Technical Primer > Chapter 1: Nodes and Communication > 1.3 Definition: Message
chunk_text: Distributed Systems: A Short Technical Primer > Chapter 1: Nodes and Communication > 1.3 Definition: Message\\n\\n1.3 Definition: Message\\n\\nA **message** is a unit of information exchanged between nodes. Message passing is the communication mechanism used by the nodes in this primer.\\n\\nA node sends a message to another node. The receiving node processes the message and may send a response.

heading: 1.4 Acronym: RPC
section_path: Distributed Systems: A Short Technical Primer > Chapter 1: Nodes and Communication > 1.4 Acronym: RPC
chunk_text: Distributed Systems: A Short Technical Primer > Chapter 1: Nodes and Communication > 1.4 Acronym: RPC\\n\\n1.4 Acronym: RPC\\n\\n**Remote Procedure Call (RPC)** is a mechanism that lets one process invoke an operation exposed by another process. In this fixture, RPC is a communication mechanism; the acronym must not be extracted from the metadata comments above.

heading: 2.1 Consensus
section_path: Distributed Systems: A Short Technical Primer > Chapter 2: Coordination and Reliability > 2.1 Consensus
chunk_text: Distributed Systems: A Short Technical Primer > Chapter 2: Coordination and Reliability > 2.1 Consensus\\n\\n2.1 Consensus\\n\\n**Consensus** is a process through which multiple nodes agree on a value or decision. Consensus protocols help coordinate replicated state.

heading: 2.2 Raft
section_path: Distributed Systems: A Short Technical Primer > Chapter 2: Coordination and Reliability > 2.2 Raft
chunk_text: Distributed Systems: A Short Technical Primer > Chapter 2: Coordination and Reliability > 2.2 Raft\\n\\n2.2 Raft\\n\\n**Raft** is a consensus algorithm. It uses leader election and log replication to coordinate a replicated log among participating nodes.

heading: 2.3 Replicated Log
section_path: Distributed Systems: A Short Technical Primer > Chapter 2: Coordination and Reliability > 2.3 Replicated Log
chunk_text: Distributed Systems: A Short Technical Primer > Chapter 2: Coordination and Reliability > 2.3 Replicated Log\\n\\n2.3 Replicated Log\\n\\nA **replicated log** is an ordered sequence of entries maintained across multiple nodes. In the Raft example, log replication helps participating nodes converge on the same sequence of committed entries.

heading: 2.4 Fault Tolerance
section_path: Distributed Systems: A Short Technical Primer > Chapter 2: Coordination and Reliability > 2.4 Fault Tolerance
chunk_text: Distributed Systems: A Short Technical Primer > Chapter 2: Coordination and Reliability > 2.4 Fault Tolerance\\n\\n2.4 Fault Tolerance\\n\\n**Fault tolerance** is the ability of a system to continue providing its intended service despite failures of some components. Replication can contribute to fault tolerance, but replication alone does not guarantee it.
